investment_summary:
Airbnb's 2025 bookings growth held, but profit did not keep pace. Revenue rose 10% to $12.2 billion and free cash flow reached $4.6 billion [1][2]. Operating margin fell to 20.8% from 23.0% as sales and marketing grew 20%, and net income dropped 5% [1].

The current price is demanding. The stock closed at $119.55 at the filing date and is now $172.15, a forward P/E of 30.8x on FY2026 consensus EPS of $5.58 [2][3]. A reverse DCF on today's enterprise value implies 9.7% annual growth for ten years at an 11.2% WACC [3]. That is below the 13.4% three-year historical CAGR and far below FY2026 consensus growth of 17.8%, so the market prices a sharp fade [1][3]. Using consensus revenue for two years and then fading growth, the implied return is 10.9%, just below the WACC [3].

The main risks are the $1.3 billion IRS claim, whose reserve falls more than $1.0 billion short, and $2.0 billion of 0% notes due March 2026, which $11.0 billion of cash covers [1][2]. Consensus data is dated after the 10-K.
key_takeaways: Margin recovery should follow as marketing growth slows toward revenue growth; operating margin fell to 20.8% from 23.0% [1].
Buybacks should keep shrinking the share count, but repurchases and related taxes of $4.36 billion absorbed most of $4.6 billion FCF [1][2].
Upside needs earnings to beat: the implied 10.9% return sits below the 11.2% WACC, so consensus EPS upgrades must hold [3].
The IRS dispute is the main cash risk: a $1.3 billion proposed tax, with the reserve more than $1.0 billion short [1].
business_overview:
Airbnb, Inc. was founded in 2007 and operates a global online marketplace for stays, experiences, and services, connecting guests and hosts in more than 220 countries and regions [1]. The company reports over 5 million hosts and 2.5 billion guest arrivals to date [1]. Scale drives the model: Nights and Seats Booked rose 8% to 533 million in 2025, and Gross Booking Value grew 12% to $91.3 billion [1]. Because service fees are collected at booking, the business generated $4.6 billion of free cash flow, a 38% margin, and held $11.0 billion of cash and short-term investments [1][2].

In May 2025 Airbnb launched services and redesigned experiences, and rolled out an app with unified search, AI personalization, Pay Less Upfront, and Reserve Now, Pay Later [1]. It also substantially completed a technology stack rebuild and expanded AI use in fraud detection and customer service [1]. The AirCover for Hosts program provides property damage protection of up to $3 million per stay [1]. During 2025 the company repurchased $3.8 billion of stock, or 29.7 million shares, with $5.6 billion remaining under its authorization [1].

At the filing date the stock closed at $119.55, within a 52-week range of $99.88 to $163.93, giving a market capitalization of $69.8 billion [2]. The price has since moved to $172.15. The consensus rating is Buy, with an average target of $205.88 and a range of $147 to $245 [3]. These consensus figures are dated after the 10-K and are used here for valuation only. Book value per share was $13.62 at the filing date [2].
market_position:
Revenue by region in 2025 was North America $5.2 billion (up 4%), EMEA $4.7 billion (up 14%), Latin America $1.2 billion (up 20%), and Asia Pacific $1.2 billion (up 17%) [1]. Roughly 61% of revenue came from outside the United States [1]. North America's share of revenue fell from 45% to 42% ($5,006 million of $11,102 million, then $5,196 million of $12,241 million), while EMEA's share rose to 39% [1]. No single city exceeded 2% of revenue [1].

The filing gives no market share figure and no customer concentration data, so share must be inferred from named competitors [1]. The 10-K names Booking Holdings, Expedia Group, Marriott, Hilton, and Viator as competitors [1]. The filing names no strategic partner beyond an unnamed data hosting provider with at least $1.7 billion of commitments through 2031 [1].

In 2025 Airbnb grew 10.3%, second of the four companies, behind Booking Holdings at 13.4% and ahead of Expedia at 7.6% and Marriott at 4.3% [4]. Growth is solid but not leading, and it is concentrated outside North America [1][4].
operating_results:
Revenue rose 10% to $12.24 billion from $11.10 billion, driven by check-ins, with Nights and Seats Booked up 8% and ADR up 3% [1]. Cost of revenue rose 11%, including $188 million of higher merchant fees, leaving gross margin near 83% [1]. Sales and marketing rose 20% to $2.59 billion, or 21% of revenue, and was the largest cost drag, with field operations and policy up 43% to $993 million [1].

Operating income was flat at $2.54 billion, so operating margin fell to 20.8% from 23.0% [1]. Product development rose 14% to $2.35 billion, and stock-based compensation rose 13% to $1.59 billion [1]. Net income fell 5% to $2.51 billion as interest income dropped $113 million to $705 million on lower rates, and net margin declined from 24% to 21% [1].

Cash generation held up. Operating cash flow rose about 3% to $4.6 billion, and capital expenditure was only $33 million, leaving free cash flow of $4.6 billion against $4.5 billion [1]. Earnings quality is the weak spot, because operating cash flow relies partly on $1.6 billion of non-cash stock compensation [1]. Consensus expects FY2026 revenue of $14.4 billion and EPS of $5.58, with EPS up 5.5% over 90 days [3]. The expected 17.8% revenue growth is well above 2025's 10.3%, and recent quarters are mixed: two beats, with the fourth-quarter 2025 result missing by 15.7% [3]. These consensus figures are dated after the 10-K.
risk_assessment:
The largest identified risk is tax. The IRS 2013 proposed adjustment could add $1.3 billion of U.S. tax plus penalties and interest, and the filing says this exceeds the current reserve by more than $1.0 billion [1]. In May 2024 the IRS issued a Notice of Deficiency for the same amount, and Airbnb petitioned the U.S. Tax Court in July 2024 [1]. Italian settlements total 894 million euros, about $957 million when the filing's dollar amounts are summed, covering 2017 to 2023 [1]. Spain has proposed a fine of about 65 million euros over short-term rental listing rules [1].

Regulation and demand are the next risks. New York City's rules amount to a de facto ban on short-term rentals, similar restrictions are under consideration across New York State, and the EU Short-Term Rental Regulation takes effect in May 2026 [1]. Travel spending falls in downturns, and revenue is recognized at check-in while costs are partly fixed, so a sudden drop in bookings reaches margins with a lag [1]. Non-U.S. dollar revenue was 56% of the 2025 total, which creates currency exposure [1]. The company also reports increasing difficulty obtaining insurance at reasonable cost, and rising premiums tied to covered claims [1].

Balance sheet liquidity needs watching. The current ratio fell to 1.38 from 1.69, because $2.00 billion of the $2.07 billion of total debt is due in March 2026 [1][2]. Equity fell to $8.20 billion, as $3.8 billion of buybacks exceeded $2.5 billion of net income [1]. Cash and short-term investments of $11.0 billion cover the notes, and a $1.0 billion revolver is undrawn [1][2]. At the latest quarter (30 September 2026), cash rose to $12.59 billion and debt to $2.41 billion [2]. The Piotroski score is 6 of 9 and the Altman Z-score is 5.26, in the safe zone [2].
competitors_analysis:
Airbnb is compared with Booking Holdings (BKNG), Expedia Group (EXPE), and Marriott International (MAR). Booking and Expedia were chosen because they run online travel marketplaces with comparable booking models, and both are named in the 10-K [1][4]. Marriott was included as a lodging company named in the 10-K. Its franchise model differs from Airbnb's, so it is a weaker comparison [1][4].

On 2025 growth, Airbnb's 10.3% trailed Booking's 13.4% but beat Expedia's 7.6% and Marriott's 4.3% [4]. Its EBITDA margin of 20.8% sits well below Booking's 40.7%, though it is above Expedia's 18.8% and Marriott's 18.3% [4]. Return on invested capital was 20.0%, the lowest of the four, compared with Booking at 50.8%, Marriott at 25.9%, and Expedia at 20.8% [4]. Gross margin of 83.0% trails Expedia's 90.1% [4]. Marriott's gross margin is calculated on a different basis, so it is not directly comparable [4].

Valuation is where the gap is largest. Airbnb's EV/EBITDA of 30.4 compares with a simple average of about 16.4 for the three peers and 15.8 for Booking [4]. Consensus forward EV/Sales is 6.3x for FY2026, and forward P/E is 30.8x on FY2026 EPS of $5.58 [3]. These figures are dated after the 10-K. On these metrics Airbnb does not screen as undervalued. Its premium depends on EBITDA growing well above the flat 2025 result, and Booking's superior margins and returns explain why the market pays more for Booking's profile than Airbnb's [4].

investment_theses.thesis: Operating margin recovers in 2026 as sales and marketing growth falls below revenue growth.
investment_theses.evidence: Sales and marketing rose 20% to $2.59 billion against revenue growth of 10%, and operating margin fell to 20.8% from 23.0% [1]. Consensus FY2026 revenue is $14.4 billion and EPS $5.58 [3].
investment_theses.signpost: In the 2026 quarterly 10-Qs, sales and marketing growth is below revenue growth in Q2 and Q3, and the FY2026 10-K shows operating margin at or above 23%.
investment_theses.invalidation: Operating margin stays below 21% in FY2026 while sales and marketing grows faster than revenue.

investment_theses.thesis: Buybacks keep shrinking the share count, funded from free cash flow.
investment_theses.evidence: Free cash flow was $4.6 billion. Buybacks of $3.8 billion plus $561 million of taxes on net share settlement totaled $4.36 billion against that FCF [1][2]. Shares outstanding fell 3.4% year on year to 602 million [2].
investment_theses.signpost: Quarterly share count falls below 589 million by the Q4 2026 report, and repurchases stay at or below free cash flow in each 2026 quarter.
investment_theses.invalidation: Repurchases exceed free cash flow for two consecutive quarters, or the share count rises.

investment_theses.thesis: The stock needs consensus earnings to keep rising, because the current valuation implies returns close to the cost of capital.
investment_theses.evidence: The reverse DCF implies 9.7% annual growth over ten years, and the implied 10.9% return is below the 11.2% WACC [3]. EPS surprises were +11.0%, +9.5%, -14.1%, and -15.7% across the last four quarters [3].
investment_theses.signpost: The Q2 2026 (June quarter) EPS beats estimates, and FY2026 consensus EPS rises above $5.58 by the Q3 2026 report.
investment_theses.invalidation: Downward estimate revisions outnumber upward revisions over 30 days, or another quarterly EPS miss occurs.

investment_theses.thesis: The IRS dispute is resolved without a cash payment above the existing reserve.
investment_theses.evidence: The IRS proposes $1.3 billion of additional tax, and the filing says this exceeds the reserve by more than $1.0 billion [1]. Cash and short-term investments of $11.0 billion cover the $2.0 billion of notes due March 2026 [1][2].
investment_theses.signpost: A Tax Court ruling or settlement is disclosed in a 2026 10-Q or 10-K, with a payment at or below the existing reserve.
investment_theses.invalidation: A ruling for the IRS requires a cash payment above $1 billion, or cash and short-term investments fall below total debt.
